## Motivation and Research Question

I recently started learning SQL and wanted to share how efficient it is when we need to connects different tables and group the specific data. This tutorial will discuss the question: **Will father with a higher income lead to child with a higher income?** We will use SQL to builds the father-child matched dataset. And use Python to estimates the regressions.

## Data and Method

I use the [Panel Study of Income Dynamics](https://psidonline.isr.umich.edu/) and its Family Identification Mapping System (FIMS). “Children” are adult sons and daughters. The selected 1994–2023 survey waves report income for 1993–2022. Their labor-income variables exclude farm and unincorporated business income. Restricting the period avoids combining these with earlier, broader totals.

Both models use the same pairs. For the single-year model, I compare both generations at approximate age **36**, usually in different calendar years. Among candidate ages 30–45, this age provides the most pairs eligible for both models. Selection uses counts, not regression coefficients. Age is survey age minus one; no additional controls enter the regression.

For the second model, each person's income is averaged within **ages 29–43**, requiring at least three observations. Each annual amount is first converted to 2022 dollars by multiplying it by the ratio of 2022 CPI to that income year's CPI. The source is [BLS CPI-U](https://www.bls.gov/developers/).

Income at one age may poorly represent lifetime income, creating life-cycle bias. Matching ages reduces age mismatch, but temporary unemployment or a bonus can still distort a single observation. Averaging smooths these fluctuations without guaranteeing removal of all bias. [Mazumder's review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6820674/) explains why longer income histories matter.

We estimate the intergenerational income elasticity, or IGE:

$$
\log(Y_{child,i})=\alpha+\beta\log(Y_{father,i})+\varepsilon_i.
$$

The slope $\beta$ measures the percentage difference in children's income associated with a 1% difference in fathers' income. For the average model, we average real incomes **before** taking logs.

## 1. Load and Match the People

The repository's `code/analysis.py` prepares four SQLite tables: `people`, `relationships`, `person_year`, and `cpi`. Permanent person IDs combine the 1968 family ID and person number. Annual family IDs help identify household records but cannot track individuals across years. Python loads prepared tables with pandas:

```python
import sqlite3
connection = sqlite3.connect("")
people.to_sql("people", connection, index=False)
```

The snippets illustrate the core operations; the complete script supplies the inputs and intermediate tables. FIMS identifies the biological father. We then check that both people exist:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT r.child_id, r.father_id
FROM relationships AS r
JOIN people AS c ON r.child_id = c.person_id
JOIN people AS p ON r.father_id = p.person_id;
```

`SELECT` chooses columns. `JOIN` connects matching IDs. The aliases `c` and `p` let us use `people` twice. Inner joins retain only pairs with both members present; `DISTINCT` removes duplicate links.

## 2. Select Each Person's Own Income

Income fields depend on household role. A child recorded as a spouse needs that person's spouse income, not the household reference person's income:

```sql
SELECT person_id, survey_year,
       CASE
           WHEN sequence_number = 1 AND relationship = 10
               THEN head_income
           WHEN sequence_number = 2 AND relationship IN (20, 22)
               THEN spouse_income
       END AS nominal_income
FROM person_year
WHERE family_id > 0;
```

`CASE` chooses the field; `WHERE` filters records. The full query also joins CPI by income year and removes invalid income codes.

## 3. Aggregate and Attach Income

The single-year query selects age 36, keeping the earlier year if that approximate age repeats. The average-income query is:

```sql
SELECT person_id, AVG(real_income) AS mean_income,
       COUNT(*) AS n_years
FROM income
WHERE age BETWEEN 29 AND 43
GROUP BY person_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
```

`GROUP BY` collects each person's observations. `AVG()` summarizes income; `COUNT()` records coverage. `HAVING` filters after aggregation. Joining this table twice attaches father and child averages. Attaching both single-year measures completes one row per pair. All four measures must be positive for logarithms; recorded zeros remain in averages.

## 4. Estimate in Python

For each model, Python runs unweighted OLS with an intercept:

```python
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.api import OLS, add_constant

x = add_constant(np.log(sample["father_mature"]))
y = np.log(sample["child_mature"])
model = OLS(y, x).fit()
```

Replacing these columns with `father_average` and `child_average` estimates the second IGE. Run `python code/analysis.py` to reproduce the workflow and save tables and figures.

## Results and Takeaway

<!-- RESULTS_START -->

Both models use **143 pairs and 123 fathers**.

| Income measure | IGE |
|---|---:|
| Single year at age 36 | 0.220 |
| Average at ages 29–43 | 0.297 |

![Income associations. Dots are group means; lines are OLS fits using individual pairs.](figures/single_vs_average.png)

<!-- RESULTS_END -->

The average-income estimate is higher. This is consistent with smoothing noisy income measurements, but it does not prove that life-cycle bias has disappeared. The practical lesson is that correct SQL matching and income definitions both matter: using the same people does not make different income measures interchangeable.

## Limitations

The fifteen-age window contains only 6.4 observations per father and 5.1 per child on average, spanning about eight years. These are incomplete lifetime-income proxies. The small, unweighted sample requires positive selected incomes and reference-person or spouse records. Imputed income and ambiguous zeros remain concerns. CPI does not remove historical labor-market differences. Results describe associations, not causal effects; no formal significance claim is made.
